ch1_10.quiz_q3_explanation: A bridge flips the negative half of the AC waveform up so it adds to the positive half instead of being thrown away. With a given smoothing capacitor, ripple is roughly halved compared to the half-wave version.
ch1_10.quiz_q4: Why is a Zener diode deliberately operated in reverse breakdown?
ch1_10.quiz_q4_a: It happens to conduct more current that way
ch1_10.quiz_q4_b: Only to rectify AC into smooth DC
ch1_10.quiz_q4_c: It only works in reverse — forward bias destroys it
ch1_10.quiz_q4_d: Its reverse-breakdown voltage is sharp and stable
ch1_10.quiz_q4_explanation: A Zener's reverse-breakdown is engineered to a specific voltage (e.g. 3.3 V, 5.1 V, 12 V) and to be sharp — past that point, the voltage stays nearly constant over a wide current range. With a series resistor to limit current, that gives you a fixed reference voltage almost for free.
ch1_10.quiz_q5: A relay coil is switched off by a transistor. Without a flyback diode across the coil, what happens?
ch1_10.quiz_q5_a: Nothing — the transistor simply shrugs it off
ch1_10.quiz_q5_b: A big voltage spike appears that can destroy the transistor
ch1_10.quiz_q5_c: The relay contacts visibly arc and spark
ch1_10.quiz_q5_d: The main supply rail slowly climbs above its rated maximum
ch1_10.quiz_q5_explanation: V = −L (di/dt). When the transistor opens, current through the coil tries to keep flowing; with nowhere to go, the coil generates whatever voltage it takes to push it through — often hundreds of volts. The flyback diode catches that current and recirculates it through the coil until the energy dissipates.
ch1_10.quiz_q6: A red LED with a forward drop of about 2 V is run from a 5 V supply. What series resistor sets the current to roughly 10 mA?
ch1_10.quiz_q6_a: No resistor is needed — the LED limits its own current
ch1_10.quiz_q6_explanation: The resistor drops the difference between the supply and the LED’s forward voltage: (5 V − 2 V) / 0.01 A = 300 Ω. A diode does not limit its own current — above its forward voltage it behaves like a near-short, so without the resistor the LED draws whatever the supply can deliver and burns out.
ch1_10.quiz_q7: In a power supply, a large capacitor is connected in parallel with the load right after the rectifier. What is its job?
ch1_10.quiz_q7_a: It charges at the peaks and feeds the load between them
ch1_10.quiz_q7_b: It blocks the DC so that only AC reaches the load
ch1_10.quiz_q7_c: It raises the output well above the peak of the rectified wave
ch1_10.quiz_q7_d: It converts the pulsing DC back into clean AC
ch1_10.quiz_q7_explanation: The reservoir capacitor stores charge at each peak of the rectified waveform and releases it into the load during the gaps between peaks. The leftover wobble is the ripple; a larger capacitor (or a lighter load) holds the voltage up better and shrinks it. It cannot push the average above the peak.
ch1_10.quiz_q8: Why is a Schottky diode often chosen for a switching power supply or a high-frequency rectifier?
ch1_10.quiz_q8_a: It has a much higher forward voltage drop than ordinary silicon
ch1_10.quiz_q8_b: It holds a constant voltage, like a Zener reference
ch1_10.quiz_q8_c: It passes only alternating current, never DC
ch1_10.quiz_q8_d: Its forward drop is low (~0.3 V) and it switches off fast
ch1_10.quiz_q8_explanation: A Schottky diode uses a metal-to-semiconductor junction, giving a forward drop of about 0.3 V (versus ~0.7 V for silicon) and almost no recovery delay when it switches off. Less voltage dropped means less heat, and fast recovery means it keeps up with high switching frequencies — exactly what a switch-mode supply needs.

ch1_11.heroAriaLabel: Pen-and-ink sketch of a TO-92 plastic-package transistor on the left with three labelled leads (collector, base, emitter), and on the right the schematic NPN symbol with an arrow showing that the part on the workbench and the circle-with-arrow in a circuit diagram are the same object.
ch1_11.intro1: Diodes were the first non-linear part in this course; the transistor is the first active one. «Active» means it can amplify: a small signal applied to one terminal controls a much larger current at another, and the extra power comes from the supply rail. Every receiver, every transmitter, every microcontroller, and every integrated circuit on a modern board is, underneath, an arrangement of transistors. Get this chapter right and the rest of radio circuit design becomes assembly rather than mystery.
ch1_11.intro2: Two big families do the work. The bipolar junction transistor (BJT) is current-controlled — a small base current sets a much larger collector current. The field-effect transistor (FET) is voltage-controlled — a gate voltage sets the drain current, with no DC gate current at all. Both come in two polarities (NPN/PNP for BJTs; n-channel/p-channel for FETs). And both do the same handful of jobs: switch (fully on or fully off, the basis of all digital logic), amplify (somewhere in between, the basis of every analog signal path), and — with a loop of feedback wrapped around the amplifier — oscillate (generate a signal out of nothing, which is how every transmitter and receiver starts).
ch1_11.familiesIntro: Four symbols cover almost everything you will meet on a hobbyist schematic — they are shown below. <jfetT>JFETs</jfetT> exist too but are uncommon outside of low-noise audio and RF front ends.
ch1_11.familiesSymbolPanelCaption: The four common transistor symbols. The arrow in each one tells you the polarity: outward-pointing emitter / inward-pointing body arrow = N-type carriers (electrons); inward-pointing emitter / outward-pointing body arrow = P-type carriers (holes). For BJTs the arrow is on the emitter; for MOSFETs it is on the source-side body terminal. The broken channel line on the MOSFET marks enhancement mode — the channel does not conduct until the gate is biased.
ch1_11.familiesAfter: BJTs and FETs are not interchangeable in detail, but for a beginner's mental model they do the same job in slightly different ways:
ch1_11.familiesBjtRow: BJT (NPN, PNP). Base–emitter junction acts like a diode (~0.7 V drop when on); a small base current I_B controls a much larger collector current I_C via I_C = β·I_B. Cheap, fast, low-noise. The bench-favourite small-signal NPN is the 2N3904 (β ≈ 100–300, max I_C = 200 mA).
ch1_11.familiesFetRow: MOSFET (n-channel, p-channel). Gate is insulated from the channel — DC gate current is essentially zero. Drain current sets the drain current and is set by V_{GS} − V_{th} (gate voltage above threshold). Excellent at high current and high speed. The bench-favourite logic-level n-MOSFET is the 2N7000 (V_{th} ≈ 2 V, max I_D = 200 mA).
ch1_11.insideIntro: Before we build circuits with it, let us look inside the transistor itself. An NPN BJT is a three-layer sandwich of doped silicon: a narrow N-type emitter on one side, a very thin P-type base in the middle, and a larger N-type collector on the other side. The geometry — and especially how thin the base is — explains everything the device does.
ch1_11.insideMechanism: To make a transistor conduct, you apply two voltages from an external power source (a battery or supply): a small V_{BE} ≈ 0.7 V between base and emitter (base positive) and a much larger V_{CE} — a few volts — between collector and emitter (collector positive). Each plays its own role. V_{BE} turns on the base-emitter junction the same way a forward voltage turns on a diode (chapter 1.10). The emitter starts to «emit» electrons into the base — hence its name. The base is so thin that almost all these electrons do not «get lost» inside it and pass straight through to the base-collector junction. There they meet a strong electric field created by V_{CE} — the field instantly «sweeps» each electron out through the collector contact, out of the transistor. Only a tiny fraction (about 1 in β+1, where β is a parameter of the specific transistor, typically 50–500) recombines inside the base — meets a hole in the P-layer and disappears as a free carrier. This tiny stream forms the base current i_b. The rest (β in β+1, i.e. almost all the electrons) reach the collector and form the collector current i_c — β times larger than i_b. This β-fold ratio is the whole essence of transistor amplification. The widget below shows this directly — turn up V_{BE} and the stream of electrons from emitter to collector grows; change β and the fraction lost in the base changes.
ch1_11.insideTwoLawsIntro: Two independent laws govern the device at the same time, one for voltage and one for current.
ch1_11.insideTwoLawsVoltage: Voltage law. The base-emitter junction behaves like an ordinary diode: a small increase in voltage produces a steep (exponential — recall the diode current-voltage curve from chapter 1.10) increase in current. Because of that, V_{BE} self-pins to a narrow band of ~0.6–0.8 V even when the current through it changes by orders of magnitude. In everyday circuit calculations this is rounded to a constant V_{BE} ≈ 0.7 V.
ch1_11.insideTwoLawsCurrent: Current law. i_c = β·i_b — the collector current is β times the base current. This is a property of the transistor itself: how thin the base is and what fraction of electrons reach the collector.
ch1_11.insideTwoLawsCompete: These laws govern different aspects of the device and never «compete»: one pins <var>V_{BE}</var> to a narrow band, the other scales <var>i_b</var> up into a much larger <var>i_c</var>.
ch1_11.insideTwoLawsWidget: Why the widget lets you slide V_{BE}. In a real circuit you do not set V_{BE} directly — it settles wherever the surrounding resistors put it. Here we drive it directly so you can see the device's response: the slider covers only 0.4–0.85 V because outside that narrow window the transistor is either fully off or in saturation.
ch1_11.insideRegions: Three regions of operation emerge naturally from the same model. Cutoff: V_{BE} is less than ~0.6 V, the junction is closed, virtually no current flows — this is «transistor off». Active: 0.6 V ≲ V_{BE} ≲ 0.75 V, the collector current is directly proportional to the base current: i_c = β·i_b — this is where amplification lives. Saturation: V_{BE} is so high that the external load (R_C and V_{CC}) can no longer supply β·i_b — current is now capped by the load, not by β. We will see all three regions in the sections that follow: switches operate at cutoff ↔ saturation, amplifiers live in the active region.
ch1_11.bjtSwitchIntro: The simplest job a transistor can do is the same one as a relay: let a small signal turn a much larger current on and off. A logic-level output from a microcontroller can source about 10 mA at 3.3 V — not enough to light a power LED, drive a motor, or energise a relay coil. A single NPN BJT bridges the gap.
ch1_11.bjtSwitchSchematicCaption: BJT switch driving an LED. Q1 is a 2N3904 small-signal NPN. When the V_{in} terminal goes to logic HIGH (3.3 V — a typical microcontroller output), current through base resistor R_b turns the transistor ON: Q1 enters saturation (V_{CE} ≈ 0.2 V) and effectively shorts the LED's bottom terminal to ground. Current then flows around the loop V_{CC} → R_c → LED → Q1 → ground, with R_c setting the LED current (not the transistor).
ch1_11.bjtSwitchHowItWorks: Walk the circuit. Input HIGH → base sits at 3.3 − 0.7 = 2.6 V above the bottom of R_b (the base-emitter junction is a diode, drops ~0.7 V), so base current is I_B = 2.6 V / R_b. The transistor would like to push β·I_B through the collector — but the collector path can only carry as much as R_c + the LED allow. The transistor goes into saturation: V_{CE} drops to ~0.2 V, and the actual collector current is set by the load (R_c + LED), not by β. As long as β·I_B ≥ I_C(load) the transistor stays saturated and acts as a closed switch (emitter grounded).
ch1_11.bjtSwitchWhyRb: Why R_b at all — what happens without it? The base-emitter junction is an ordinary silicon diode (chapter 1.10): when current flows through it in the forward direction, V_{BE} stays around 0.7 V regardless of how much current is flowing. If you wire the microcontroller pin directly to the base (no R_b), you are applying 3.3 V to a junction that can only hold 0.7 V across itself. The «excess» 2.6 V has nowhere to drop, and the current through the junction is limited only by the small internal resistance of the microcontroller pin and the tiny resistance of the diode itself. This is essentially a short circuit through a diode: tens or hundreds of mA flow into the base — far above the safe current for the microcontroller pin (typically ~20–25 mA) and for the base-emitter junction of a small-signal transistor (~100 mA). The microcontroller pin burns out, the transistor's base-emitter junction overheats and the transistor dies — often both at once. R_b converts the problem from «apply a voltage» into «set a current»: with R_b in series in the base lead, the 2.6 V «excess» drops across R_b instead of the diode, and I_B is set by Ohm's law: I_B = 2.6 V / R_b — a predictable, designable number. Without R_b the circuit has no current control: it is not «slightly suboptimal», it is a guaranteed failure as soon as you power up.
ch1_11.bjtSwitchKey: Sizing rule. Pick I_C from the load (e.g. 10 mA for an LED). Assume a worst-case β = 50 (2N3904 is rated 100+ but vary widely). Pick I_B = 5 × I_C / β — that's a generous 5× overdrive to keep the transistor saturated even on a low-β specimen. Then R_b = (V_{in} − 0.7) / I_B. For a 3.3 V logic input driving 10 mA: I_B = 5 × 10 / 50 = 1 mA, so R_b = 2.6 V / 1 mA = 2.6 kΩ — round down to a standard 2.2 kΩ resistor for a comfortable margin.
ch1_11.bjtSwitchTip: Why a transistor and not just a wire? Three reasons. (1) Current amplification — a 1 mA microcontroller pin commands a 10–500 mA load. (2) Voltage translation — the input side runs on 3.3 V, the load can run on 5 V, 12 V, or 24 V. (3) Speed and life — a transistor switch lasts forever and switches in nanoseconds; mechanical relays click, wear out, and bounce. Computer-controlled anything (motors, relays, LEDs, lasers) sits on top of this one circuit.
ch1_11.bjtSwitchInductiveCaution: Inductive loads need a flyback diode. If the load is a relay coil, motor, or any wound element, repeat the rule from Chapter 1.10: put a flyback diode (cathode to V_{CC}) across the coil. Without it, the inductor's collapsing field will spike to 200+ V when the transistor turns OFF, and the spike walks straight into V_{CE} and destroys the part.
ch1_11.mosfetSwitchIntro: Same job, different controls. Replace the BJT with an n-channel enhancement MOSFET (e.g. 2N7000 for small loads, IRLZ44N for power) and the base resistor disappears: the gate is insulated, so DC gate current is essentially zero. Just connect the logic input directly to the gate.
ch1_11.mosfetSwitchSchematicCaption: MOSFET low-side switch driving the same LED. Q1 is a logic-level n-MOSFET (e.g. 2N7000). The gate connects directly to the input — no base resistor needed for DC. The optional R_g (typically 100 Ω) is there to tame switching transients in fast circuits and is not required for slow on/off control.
ch1_11.mosfetSwitchVsBjt: BJT vs MOSFET as a switch — when to use which.
ch1_11.mosfetSwitchVsBjtBjt: BJT has no clear technical edge over a logic-level MOSFET as a low-current switch — any modern logic-level MOSFET turns fully on from 3.3 V and has a lower on-resistance. The BJT-as-switch survives for pragmatic reasons: the 2N3904 sits in every starter kit, the base-emitter junction is far more tolerant of electrostatic discharge than a MOSFET's thin gate oxide, and V_{BE} is predictable from specimen to specimen (~0.7 V), whereas MOSFET V_{th} can vary by a factor of 3–4× (the 2N7000 datasheet quotes 0.8 V to 3.0 V). Above ~100 mA the BJT loses decisively on power dissipation.
ch1_11.mosfetSwitchVsBjtMosfet: MOSFET wins everywhere else, especially at currents above ~100 mA. The on-resistance R_{DS(on)} is often a few milliohms — a 10 A load through a 5 mΩ MOSFET dissipates only 0.5 W, where a BJT at the same current would burn 2 W and need a heatsink. This is why every motor driver, every solid-state relay, and every laptop battery management chip uses MOSFETs.
ch1_11.mosfetSwitchLogicLevel: «Logic-level» matters. An ordinary MOSFET needs ~5 V on the gate to turn fully on; a 3.3 V logic output will not pull it past V_{th} and you will get a half-on transistor that dissipates a lot of heat. Logic-level MOSFETs (datasheet quotes R_{DS(on)} at V_{GS} = 2.5 V or 3 V) are designed for direct microcontroller drive. Look for parts whose name ends in L — a part number ending in L rather than F (e.g. International Rectifier’s logic-level family).
ch1_11.sectionCurves: Output curves and the active region
ch1_11.curvesIntro: Switching is the easy half — the transistor lives at the two extremes of its behaviour, fully off or fully on. The other half is amplification, where it lives between the extremes. To see what «between» means, plot the transistor's output characteristic curves. On the graph below the horizontal axis is V_{CE} (collector-emitter voltage) and the vertical axis is I_C (collector current). The base current I_B does NOT have its own axis — instead it chooses which curve we see: each of the four curves is plotted for a single fixed value of I_B (10, 20, 30, and 40 µA respectively), and a larger I_B places the curve higher. This is called a «family of characteristics» — a stack of curves drawn for different values of one parameter.
ch1_11.curvesDiagramAria: Plot of BJT output characteristic curves: collector current versus collector-emitter voltage, repeated for several values of base current. The plane is divided into a saturation region (left strip), a cutoff region (bottom strip), and an active region where the curves are nearly flat.
ch1_11.curvesDiagramCaption: BJT output curves. Each curve shows how I_C varies with V_{CE} at a fixed base current I_B. The family of curves divides the operating plane into three regions: cutoff (no base current — collector current is essentially zero), saturation (V_{CE} below ~0.2 V — current is limited by the load, not by β), and active (the flat region where I_C is set by I_B and barely depends on V_{CE}). For amplification we operate the transistor in the active region, where the curves are nearly flat and a small change in I_B moves the curves up or down by β times that change.
ch1_11.curvesWhatChangesVce: One natural question: what changes V_{CE}? It is not a knob you turn directly. In a real circuit, V_{CE} is the voltage «left over» on the transistor after R_C drops its share of the supply: V_{CE} = V_{CC} − I_C·R_C. To shift V_{CE} you change V_{CC}, R_C, or the current through the circuit — not V_{CE} directly. So how is the graph above actually made? By a piece of test equipment called a curve tracer. It has two independent control channels: one sets I_B to a chosen value (using an internal current source — unlike a normal circuit where I_B is set indirectly through R_b), and the other sweeps V_{CE} from 0 V upward while measuring the resulting I_C. Then the instrument steps to the next I_B value and draws the next curve. Which (V_{CE}, I_C) point a real amplifier design actually lands on — is determined by the load line, the topic of the next subsection.
ch1_11.curvesActiveRegion: Active region — the flat part of each curve, where V_{CE} is at least ~0.5 V. That is enough for the electric field on the collector side (the same physics described in «How the transistor actually works») to sweep every electron that reaches the base out through the collector. Here the transistor behaves like a current source: I_C ≈ β·I_B, almost independent of V_{CE}. Each curve is a different setting of that current source.
ch1_11.curvesSaturation: Saturation — the steep left edge, where V_{CE} is below ~0.2 V. The transistor wants to push β·I_B through the collector but cannot — the load is in the way. Current is set by Ohm's law on the load, not by the transistor. This is the «closed switch» mode we used in the previous section.
ch1_11.curvesCutoff: Cutoff — base current is zero (or below the ~0.6 V turn-on threshold), so collector current is also zero except for tiny leakage. This is the «open switch» mode.
ch1_11.sectionLoadLine: The load line — finding the operating point
ch1_11.loadLineIntro: A transistor's output characteristic shows what current I_C it is able to pass for any given V_{CE} and I_B — but that is only a set of possible states. The characteristic alone cannot tell you which point on that curve the transistor actually lands on in a specific circuit — for that you need a second condition, set by the external circuit (the supply V_{CC} and the collector resistor R_C). The classical approach is to overlay a load line on top of the characteristics — a straight line representing that external constraint. The real current and voltage settle exactly where the load line meets the characteristic for the current I_B.
ch1_11.loadLineDerivation: Derive the load line. Walk around the collector loop with Kirchhoff's voltage law: V_{CC} = I_C·R_C + V_{CE}. Solve for I_C: I_C = (V_{CC} − V_{CE}) / R_C. That is a straight line on the (V_{CE}, I_C) plane with slope −1/R_C, x-intercept V_{CC} (when I_C = 0, transistor in cutoff), and y-intercept V_{CC}/R_C (when V_{CE} = 0, transistor in saturation). The actual operating point — the Q-point (quiescent point) — is the intersection of this load line with whichever output curve corresponds to the chosen base current.
ch1_11.loadLineQpointKey: The Q-point story in three sentences. The transistor's curves say what I_C the device could deliver at a given V_{CE} for each I_B. The load line says what V_{CE} the rest of the circuit permits at a given I_C. The intersection — one point — is what actually happens.
ch1_11.loadLineSwingNote: Why bias to mid-rail. Place the Q-point in the middle of the load line — at V_{CE} ≈ V_{CC}/2 — and the output can swing equal distances up (toward V_{CC}, cutoff) and down (toward 0 V, saturation) without clipping. Bias too close to either end and one half of the signal hits the rail. The widget below lets you slide the Q-point and see where it clips.
ch1_11.ceIntro: Now turn the static Q-point into a working amplifier. Hold the Q-point at mid-rail with a bias network, then add a small AC signal in a common-emitter stage on top of the steady base current. The transistor's collector current wiggles around the Q-point by β times that signal, and the wiggle drops across R_C as a (much larger) voltage swing on the collector.
ch1_11.ceSchematicCaption: Common-emitter amplifier with voltage-divider bias. <var>R_1</var> and <var>R_2</var> form a divider that holds the base steady at ~<nowrap>(<var>R_2</var>/(<var>R_1</var>+<var>R_2</var>))·<var>V_{CC}</var></nowrap>. <var>R_E</var> sets the emitter current — and therefore <var>I_C</var> — through Ohm's law. <var>R_C</var> turns that current into an output voltage. <var>C_{in}</var> blocks DC from the source while passing AC to the base; <var>C_{out}</var> blocks the DC offset on the collector while passing the AC signal to the next stage.
ch1_11.ceGainStory: The gain formula. An AC wiggle v_{in} at the base appears, almost unchanged, at the emitter (V_{BE} is pinned to ~0.7 V, so the emitter «follows» the base — any change at the base shows up at the emitter with the same offset). This voltage drops across R_E, producing — by Ohm's law — an emitter current wiggle i_e = v_{in}/R_E. Almost all of that becomes collector current (β is large, so i_c ≈ i_e). Now follow i_c in the circuit: it flows from the fixed V_{CC} rail down through R_C into the collector, so by Ohm's law it drops a voltage i_c·R_C on R_C. Since V_{CC} itself does not move, every extra volt dropped on R_C is a volt subtracted from the collector. The AC component at the collector is therefore v_{out} = −i_c·R_C = −v_{in}·(R_C/R_E) — the minus sign is where phase inversion comes from. So the voltage gain is
ch1_11.ceGainAfter: The minus sign means phase inversion: a positive wiggle at the input becomes a negative wiggle at the output. The ratio R_C/R_E is the gain magnitude — typically 10–100 for one transistor. Importantly, β does not appear in the formula: as long as β is «big enough» for the approximation i_c ≈ i_e to hold, the gain depends only on resistor ratios, which are stable across temperature and across different specimens of the same transistor.
ch1_11.ceWorkedExample: Worked example. Pick V_{CC} = 9 V (a typical battery), R_C = 4.7 kΩ, R_E = 470 Ω, divider R_1 = 47 kΩ + R_2 = 10 kΩ. The divider holds the base at 9·10/(47+10) ≈ 1.6 V; subtract V_{BE} = 0.7 V → emitter at 0.9 V → emitter current I_E = 0.9/470 ≈ 1.9 mA. Collector takes the same 1.9 mA, dropping 1.9·4.7 ≈ 9 V across R_C. Wait — that's the whole supply! Reduce R_C to 2.2 kΩ → drop is 4.2 V → collector sits at 9 − 4.2 = 4.8 V, comfortably mid-rail. Gain is then −2200/470 ≈ −4.7: a 100 mV signal at the input becomes a 470 mV inverted signal at the output. The widget below lets you tune the values and watch gain, Q-point, and maximum output swing all change together.
ch1_11.ceClippingNote: Clipping. If the input swing is large enough to push the Q-point past either end of the load line, the output flattens at V_{CC} (cutoff) or near 0 V (saturation). That's distortion — the same kind that turns a clean guitar into a fuzz pedal. For a faithful amplifier, keep the input small; for a deliberate hard-clipper, drive it hard. Both are useful, in different places.
ch1_11.sectionCs: Common-source FET amplifier — the FET analogue
ch1_11.csIntro: The MOSFET version of the common-emitter circuit is the common-source amplifier: gate replaces base, drain replaces collector, source replaces emitter. The schematic looks identical with FET symbols swapped in. The gain formula is
ch1_11.csGainAfter: where transconductance g_m = δI_D/δV_{GS} takes the role of «1/R_E» in the BJT formula. For a 2N7000 at a few mA, g_m is on the order of 50 mS (millisiemens, i.e. 0.05 A/V), giving gains of −5 to −20 with kΩ-range drain resistors. FETs amplify like BJTs but with two practical wins: infinite DC input impedance (the gate draws no current, so you can drive it from very weak sources) and no shot noise from base current (the noise floor is dominated by channel thermal noise, much lower at audio frequencies). The trade-off is that g_m values are smaller than the equivalent 1/R_E in a BJT, so a single-stage CS amplifier typically has lower gain than its CE counterpart at the same currents.
ch1_11.sectionBias: Why biasing is hard — and how the divider rescues us
ch1_11.biasIntro: We waved hands earlier when we said «hold the Q-point at mid-rail with a bias network». Why is that hard? Because the BJT's most useful parameter — β — is its least reliable: a 2N3904 datasheet quotes β between 100 and 300 (factor of three at the same current), β changes by 30–50 % from cold to hot, and two transistors from the same reel can differ by 50 %. A bias scheme that depends on a specific β cannot work — the same circuit with a different transistor would put the Q-point in saturation or cutoff.
ch1_11.biasFix: The voltage-divider + emitter-resistor scheme used above is the standard fix. The divider sets the base voltage (not the base current) at a value that does not depend on β. The emitter resistor sets the emitter current by Ohm's law on V_E, which also does not depend on β. So I_C ≈ I_E is set by passive components only, β cancels out of the answer, and the Q-point lands where you placed it regardless of which 2N3904 you grabbed from the bin. This is why the four-resistor common-emitter circuit is the textbook standard — it is the simplest amplifier whose Q-point is β-insensitive.
ch1_11.biasTempNote: And temperature. The base-emitter voltage V_{BE} drifts about −2 mV per °C — warm a transistor by 50 °C and V_{BE} drops by 100 mV. Without R_E, that 100 mV would shift the operating point dramatically (collector current depends exponentially on V_{BE}). With R_E in place the shift just changes V_E by 100 mV, which barely budges I_E if V_E is already 1 V or so. The same emitter resistor that defeats β-spread also defeats V_{BE}-drift. One part, two problems solved.

bjtOp.title: How current flows through a BJT
bjtOp.description: Move <var>V_{BE}</var> and watch the carrier stream change. The yellow band is the thin base; carriers shooting from emitter to collector pass through it almost unhindered — only a small fraction (one in β) gets stuck and emerges as base current.
bjtOp.ariaLabel: Animated cross-section of an NPN BJT showing electron flow from emitter through the thin base to the collector. Sliders control base-emitter voltage and the current-gain factor beta.

regionDescription.cutoff: <var>V_{BE}</var> below the junction threshold (~0.6 V) — the transistor is closed, almost no current flows.
regionDescription.active: Current grows exponentially with <var>V_{BE}</var>; the ratio <nowrap><var>i_c</var>/<var>i_b</var></nowrap> stays equal to β. This is the region used for amplification.
regionDescription.saturation: The widget capped i_c at 3.5 mA to model an external-load limit. In a real circuit the load (R_C and V_{CC}) would clip the current the same way: the transistor enters saturation, V_{CE} drops to ~0.2 V, and the collector current is now set by the load rather than by β.

bjtSwitch.title: BJT switch designer
bjtSwitch.description: Pick the input voltage, target collector (load) current, and the transistor's β. The widget computes the base resistor needed to put the BJT firmly into saturation, plus the actual base and collector currents you should expect.
bjtSwitch.readoutSaturated: Transistor is firmly saturated. β·<var>I_B</var> = {{beta_ib}} ≥ <var>I_C</var> — switch is closed.
bjtSwitch.readoutNotSaturated: Warning — β·<var>I_B</var> = {{beta_ib}} is below the requested <var>I_C</var>. The transistor is in the active region, not saturation; <var>V_{CE}</var> is rising and the transistor is dissipating significant power. Lower <var>R_b</var> or pick a higher-β part.

loadLine.title: Load line and the Q-point
loadLine.description: Slide <var>V_{CC}</var>, <var>R_C</var>, and the base current. Watch the load line redraw across the family of output curves and the Q-point ride along its intersection. The shaded swing region shows how far the output can move up and down before it clips.
loadLine.ariaLabel: Plot of BJT output characteristic curves (collector current versus collector-emitter voltage for several base currents). A diagonal load line crosses them all from the supply-voltage x-intercept to the saturation-current y-intercept. An open-circle marker shows the Q-point at the intersection of the load line with the active base-current curve. A shaded band shows the available output swing around the Q-point.

ceGain.title: Common-emitter gain calculator
ceGain.description: Tune <var>V_{CC}</var>, <var>R_C</var>, <var>R_E</var>, and the divider ratio (<var>R_1</var>, <var>R_2</var>). The widget computes the Q-point (<var>V_C</var>, <var>V_E</var>, <var>I_C</var>), the small-signal voltage gain, the maximum output swing before clipping, and flags any bias that would push the transistor out of the active region.
ceGain.warnSaturated: Q-point is in saturation — V_C is below 0.5 V. The amplifier cannot follow positive input swings. Reduce R_C or raise V_{CC}.
ceGain.warnCutoff: Q-point is near cutoff — V_C is within 0.5 V of V_{CC}. The amplifier cannot follow negative input swings. Raise R_C or lower the divider voltage.
ceGain.warnGood: Q-point sits comfortably in the active region — clean swing both directions.

ch1_11.labGoal: Build the simplest practical transistor circuit — a 2N3904 NPN switch that drives an LED from a microcontroller-style logic input. Measure base and collector currents, compute β, and verify the saturation rule β·<var>I_B</var> ≥ <var>I_C</var>.
ch1_11.labEquip3: 3 V supply (two AA cells in series — the chapter's preferred lab supply)
ch1_11.labEquip4: A second pair of AA cells (or any small DC source ≥ 3 V) to double as a logic-level «input»
ch1_11.labComp1: 2N3904 NPN transistor (any small-signal NPN works — BC547 (a common European-stock NPN), 2N2222 also fine)
ch1_11.labComp2: Red LED (or any LED with <var>V_F</var> ≤ 2 V)
ch1_11.labComp3: 150 Ω collector resistor (sets ~6 mA through the LED at 3 V)
ch1_11.labComp4: 10 kΩ base resistor (deliberately oversized, to check that the saturation rule still holds with a much weaker base drive)
ch1_11.labComp5: 1 kΩ base resistor (the «right» value for this circuit)
ch1_11.labStep1: Wire the switch on the breadboard. +3 V rail → 150 Ω → LED anode → LED cathode → collector. Emitter → ground. Separately: logic input → 1 kΩ → base. Pinout of a 2N3904 looking at the flat side with leads pointing down: left = emitter, middle = base, right = collector.
ch1_11.labStep2: Connect the «logic input» wire to ground. The LED should be off. With the multimeter in DC mA mode, measure the current flowing through the base resistor (break the circuit at one end of the 1 kΩ and put the meter in series). It should read 0 mA.
ch1_11.labStep3: Switch the input from ground to +3 V. The LED lights up. Measure the base current the same way as in step 2 — it should be ~2.3 mA (= (3 − 0.7) / 1 kΩ). Now break the collector loop and measure the collector current — it should be ~6 mA (= (<var>V_{supply}</var> − <var>V_{LED}</var> − <var>V_{CE,\mathrm{sat}}</var>) / <var>R_C</var> = (3 − 2 − 0.2) / 150 Ω). Compute the ratio β·<var>I_B</var> / <var>I_C</var>: at β = 100 (typical for the 2N3904 at this current), β·<var>I_B</var> = 230 mA, which far exceeds the 6 mA the load draws. The transistor is in deep saturation, exactly as the rule predicted.
ch1_11.labStep4: Replace the 1 kΩ base resistor with the 10 kΩ. Base current drops to ~0.23 mA. With β = 100, β·I_B is now only 23 mA, still well above the 6 mA needed — LED stays bright, transistor still saturated. Now imagine you need a 50 mA load (a small relay, say): with the 10 kΩ resistor in place, β·I_B = 23 mA is below 50 mA, the transistor cannot saturate, and most of the supply voltage gets dissipated as heat in the transistor instead of going to the load.
ch1_11.labStep5: Compute «forced β» = I_C/I_B from your measurements. This ratio is NOT the transistor's true β. With R_b = 1 kΩ (step 3): forced β ≈ 6 mA / 2.3 mA ≈ 2.6. With R_b = 10 kΩ (step 4): forced β ≈ 6 mA / 0.23 mA ≈ 26. Both are far below the device's intrinsic β (≈100–300 for the 2N3904). Why the discrepancy? In saturation, I_C is set by the load (R_C and the LED), not by β·I_B — the transistor is overdriven, the extra base current just doesn't matter. «Forced β» measures the safety margin of your switch — how much extra base drive you have over the bare minimum needed. True β is measured in the active region, with a much larger R_b and a load that lets I_C actually reach β·I_B. The 5× rule of thumb from the switch section is essentially «forced β ≥ 5 under worst-case device β».
ch1_11.labExpected: With base resistor 1 kΩ: I_B ≈ 2.3 mA, I_C ≈ 6 mA, transistor saturated, LED lit brightly. The «forced β» = I_C/I_B you measure will be about 2–3 — this is the safety margin of your switch (about 5× the bare minimum), not the device's intrinsic β. After swapping to a 10 kΩ base resistor, I_B drops to ~0.23 mA and forced β rises to ~26 — still well above 1, so the transistor stays in saturation and the LED still lights.
ch1_11.labConnection: You have just built and measured the circuit from the BJT as a switch section earlier in the chapter. The base resistor calculation, the saturation rule, and the β-spread story are all on your bench rather than on a screen. The same 2N3904 will reappear next time you build anything that switches under digital control — every motor driver, every relay board, every Arduino kit ever shipped has this circuit somewhere on its schematic.
ch1_11.labTrouble1: LED doesn't light up when the input is high: check the transistor pinout (for the 2N3904 looking at the flat side, leads pointing down: left = emitter, middle = base, right = collector; pinout can differ for other NPN transistors, so check the datasheet for any replacement). Also check LED polarity: longer lead = anode, in this circuit it connects through the 150 Ω resistor to the +3 V rail; shorter lead = cathode, it goes to the collector.
ch1_11.labTrouble2: LED is dimly lit when input is supposed to be HIGH: base resistor is too large for the current the load draws. Compute β·<var>I_B</var> and compare against the load's expected <var>I_C</var>; if the ratio is below 5–10, the transistor is in the active region (not saturation) and most of the supply is being burnt across <var>V_{CE}</var>.
ch1_11.labTrouble3: Transistor warm to the touch even at small currents: same as above — likely in active region, not saturated. Reduce <var>R_b</var> or check that the input is actually reaching +3 V (a poorly-seated jumper looks identical to a HIGH input until you measure).
ch1_11.quiz_q1: What controls the collector current in a BJT?
ch1_11.quiz_q1_a: The base–emitter voltage, directly by Ohm's law
ch1_11.quiz_q1_c: The base current flowing into the base terminal
ch1_11.quiz_q1_d: The supply rail <var>V_{CC}</var> and the collector resistor
ch1_11.quiz_q1_explanation: A BJT is a current-controlled device: I_C ≈ β·I_B. The base voltage matters only through its forward-biasing of the base-emitter junction (V_BE ≈ 0.7 V); above that threshold, what flows through the base controls what flows through the collector.
ch1_11.quiz_q2: What is the saturation region of a BJT?
ch1_11.quiz_q2_a: The region where <var>I_C</var> is set by <var>β</var>·<var>I_B</var> and barely changes with <var>V_{CE}</var>
ch1_11.quiz_q2_b: The region where <var>V_{CE}</var> has dropped to ~0.2 V and the load sets <var>I_C</var>
ch1_11.quiz_q2_c: The region where the transistor is fully switched off and no current flows
ch1_11.quiz_q2_d: The region of high <var>V_{CE}</var> where avalanche breakdown sets in
ch1_11.quiz_q2_explanation: Saturation is the steep left edge of the output curves: V_CE has been pulled to ~0.2 V and the transistor cannot push more current through the collector even though β·I_B would predict it could. In saturation the transistor acts as a closed switch — current is set by Ohm's law on the load.
ch1_11.quiz_q3: Why does the common-emitter amplifier use a divider plus an emitter resistor R_E for biasing, instead of a single base resistor?
ch1_11.quiz_q3_a: It makes the schematic look more symmetrical
ch1_11.quiz_q3_b: It always gives a higher voltage gain than other schemes
ch1_11.quiz_q3_c: It uses fewer components, so the board is cheaper to build
ch1_11.quiz_q3_d: It sets the operating point from resistor ratios, not <var>β</var>
ch1_11.quiz_q3_explanation: β can vary from 50 to 300 across specimens of the same part number, plus 30–50 % with temperature. A bias scheme that depends on β places the Q-point in the wrong place when you swap transistors. The four-resistor circuit sets V_E by Ohm's law on R_E (no β involved), and I_C ≈ I_E, so β cancels out and the operating point is stable.
ch1_11.quiz_q4: On the load-line plot, what does the Q-point represent?
ch1_11.quiz_q4_a: The maximum collector current the transistor can safely handle
ch1_11.quiz_q4_b: Where the load line crosses the chosen <var>I_B</var> curve — the resting point
ch1_11.quiz_q4_c: The operating point at which the transistor risks avalanche breakdown
ch1_11.quiz_q4_d: The peak amplitude of the amplified output signal
ch1_11.quiz_q4_explanation: The Q-point (quiescent point) is the steady-state operating point — the (<var>V_{CE}</var>, <var>I_C</var>) at which the transistor sits when the AC input is zero. It is found graphically as the intersection of the load line (set by <var>V_{CC}</var> and <var>R_C</var>) with the output curve corresponding to the chosen base current.
ch1_11.quiz_q5: What is the main advantage of a MOSFET over a BJT as a switch driving a 5 A load?
ch1_11.quiz_q5_a: Its lower purchase cost compared with an equivalent BJT
ch1_11.quiz_q5_b: Its higher current gain, so a tiny gate current controls the 5 A load
ch1_11.quiz_q5_c: Only its faster switching — the power dissipated is the same
ch1_11.quiz_q5_d: Its far lower on-state voltage drop, so it wastes much less heat
ch1_11.quiz_q5_explanation: A power MOSFET with <var>R_{DS(on}</var>) of 5 mΩ dropping 5 A wastes only 25 mV × 5 A = 125 mW. A BJT with <var>V_{CE,\mathrm{sat}}</var> of 0.2 V at 5 A wastes 1 W — eight times more, requiring a heatsink. This is why every modern power switch (motor driver, solid-state relay, battery management chip) is a MOSFET, not a BJT.
ch1_11.quiz_q6: A BJT is used as a switch. What does the cutoff region correspond to?
ch1_11.quiz_q6_a: The transistor fully on, with <var>V_{CE}</var> pulled down to about 0.2 V
ch1_11.quiz_q6_b: The active region, where <var>I_C</var> is proportional to <var>I_B</var>
ch1_11.quiz_q6_c: <var>V_{BE}</var> below about 0.6 V, so essentially no current flows
ch1_11.quiz_q6_explanation: In cutoff the base-emitter junction is not forward-biased (<var>V_{BE}</var> below ~0.6 V), so essentially no base current and therefore no collector current flow — the transistor acts like an open switch. Saturation is the opposite extreme, the «closed switch».
ch1_11.quiz_q7: What is the fundamental difference between how a BJT and a MOSFET are controlled?
ch1_11.quiz_q7_a: A BJT is controlled by base current; a MOSFET by gate voltage
ch1_11.quiz_q7_b: None — both are controlled by the current you feed into the input
ch1_11.quiz_q7_c: A MOSFET is controlled by current and a BJT by voltage
ch1_11.quiz_q7_d: Both are set purely by the supply rail <var>V_{CC}</var>
ch1_11.quiz_q7_explanation: A BJT needs a continuous base current to hold the collector current on, so it is current-controlled. A MOSFET’s gate is insulated from the channel: once charged it draws essentially no steady current, so it is voltage-controlled. That is why a MOSFET can often be driven straight from a logic pin while a BJT needs a base resistor sized for current.
ch1_11.quiz_q8: In a BJT switch, why is a resistor placed in series with the base?
ch1_11.quiz_q8_a: To limit the base current to a safe, defined value
ch1_11.quiz_q8_b: To push the collector current above <var>β</var>·<var>I_B</var>
ch1_11.quiz_q8_c: To convert the input voltage into alternating current
ch1_11.quiz_q8_d: To keep the transistor in the active region so it never saturates
ch1_11.quiz_q8_explanation: Once <var>V_{BE}</var> reaches about 0.7 V the base-emitter junction conducts like a forward-biased diode — almost a short circuit. The series base resistor limits the base current to a safe value, <var>I_B</var> = (<var>V_{in}</var> − 0.7 V) / <var>R_B</var>, chosen large enough to drive the transistor hard into saturation for clean switching.
ch1_11.ceTerminology: Why «common»? A transistor has three terminals (B, C, E), but an amplifier needs four «contacts»: two for the input and two for the output. So one terminal must be shared between the input and output loops — and which terminal is shared gives the entire configuration its name. In the circuit we are about to study, that shared terminal is the emitter: the input voltage v_{in} is measured from base «down» to ground, the output v_{out} from collector «down» to ground, and the emitter sits «at the bottom» in both cases (right on ground, or nearly so — through a small resistor R_E). Hence the name — common-emitter amplifier (CE). Two other configurations exist — common-collector (also known as the emitter follower) and common-base; both have different characteristics and are used less often.
ch1_11.ceWhyInverted: Why positive input → negative output. Let's walk through it with concrete numbers. Take V_{CC} = 9 V, R_C = 2.2 kΩ, and a bias that holds the operating point at I_C ≈ 1 mA.At rest (no input signal): drop across R_C = 1.0 · 2.2 = 2.2 V → collector voltage V_C = 9 − 2.2 = 6.8 V.Positive half-wave at the input (+0.03 V): V_{BE} is 0.03 V higher, the junction opens more, I_C grows — say to 1.5 mA. Then the drop across R_C = 1.5 · 2.2 = 3.3 V → V_C = 9 − 3.3 = 5.7 V (dropped by 1.1 V).Negative half-wave (−0.03 V): I_C falls to 0.5 mA → drop across R_C = 1.1 V → V_C = 9 − 1.1 = 7.9 V (rose by 1.1 V).So input «up» → output «down» and vice versa. Why is that? Because V_{CC} is a fixed «volt budget» that's split between two series elements — R_C and the transistor. How much R_C «takes» is set by Ohm's law (drop = I·R) and grows with the current. What's «left over» is the collector voltage — our output. The bigger the current, the more of the budget R_C eats, and the less is left for the transistor. The minus sign in v_{out} = V_{CC} − I_C·R_C is just the math of this «subtraction from the budget».
ch1_11.sectionTwoModels: Two mental models: switch and current source
ch1_11.twoModelsIntro: You have now used the transistor as a switch and seen its output characteristics — the family of curves with the flat active region in the middle. Before moving on to the load line and the common-emitter amplifier, it pays to step back and name the two separate mental models engineers use to think about this device. Which one applies depends entirely on which operating mode the transistor is in.
ch1_11.twoModelsSwitch: «Controllable resistor» model — for switching. In cutoff and saturation the transistor behaves roughly like a resistor whose resistance is controlled by the base current. I_B = 0 → resistance of megohms (open switch). I_B large → resistance falls to ones or tens of ohms (closed switch). This is the intuition for BJT switches: whether the transistor can carry the load current, how much it heats up, what the control signal needs to be. In this model, only the endpoints of the characteristic matter (far left at V_{CE} ≈ 0 or far right at V_{CE} ≈ V_{CC}).
ch1_11.twoModelsAmplifier: «Current-controlled current source» model — for amplification. In the active region the transistor behaves completely differently: it conducts a current I_C ≈ β·I_B, and that value is almost independent of the voltage V_{CE} across it. So it's not a «resistor» but a self-adjusting current regulator: whatever V_{CE} happens to be, the collector carries the same current (set by the base). For active-region work, picture the transistor as a current-controlled current source. Those horizontal plateaus you saw on the family of curves in the previous subsection are the visual cue: the transistor «holds» a particular I_C regardless of V_{CE}.
ch1_11.twoModelsBoth: Two models, one reality. These aren't different transistors or hidden settings — it's the same device living in different operating points on the family of curves. As a switch — on the «vertical walls» of the graph (V_{CE} ≈ 0 or V_{CE} ≈ V_{CC}) — that's what you saw in the switching subsections. As an amplifier — on the horizontal plateaus in between — and that's what the load line and the common-emitter sections that follow are about.
ch1_11.insideWhyEmitterInjects: Why does forward-biasing the base make the emitter inject electrons? The base current is not the cause — both the injection and I_B are consequences of the same event: forward-biasing the base-emitter junction with V_{BE}. When V_{BE} lowers the BE barrier, two diffusion flows start at once: electrons emitter → base (the emitter has plenty) and holes base → emitter (the symmetric counter-flow). The emitter is doped 100–1000× more heavily than the base, so the electron current vastly outweighs the hole current. The electrons cross the thin base and become I_C; the holes — plus the small fraction of electrons that recombine in the base — are what the external circuit must replenish through the base terminal, and that is I_B. The ratio β just measures how asymmetric the doping makes those two flows.
ch1_11.insideWhyIcIndependent: Why doesn't I_C depend on V_{CE} in the active region? Picture it as a waterfall. Electrons enter the base from the emitter at a rate set by V_{BE} — the «river». They diffuse across the thin base and reach the base-collector junction, which is reverse-biased — a strong field acting like a vacuum that instantly carries away every arriving electron. V_{CE} controls how hard each electron is yanked across the junction, but not the rate at which electrons arrive. That rate is set entirely by the river upstream. So I_C ≈ β·I_B whether V_{CE} is 1 V or 10 V — the transistor «holds» its current the same way a tap holds its drip rate regardless of how far the water then falls. The small upward slope you see on real characteristic curves (the Early effect) comes from V_{CE} slightly widening the base-collector depletion region, which slightly thins the effective base and lifts I_C by ~5–10% across the working range.
ch1_11.insideBiasNote: Forward and reverse bias. When we say one side of the junction is at a «higher potential», we mean the side connected to the «+» terminal of an external voltage source (a battery, supply, etc.). The internal carrier counts — electrons in N, holes in P — were set by doping and don't change; the external voltage simply pushes those existing carriers around. Forward bias — external «+» on the P side. The applied field counteracts the internal barrier at the junction, the barrier drops, and majority carriers from both sides can diffuse across — this is what V_{BE} does to the base-emitter junction, and the same way a diode «opens» in chapter 1.10. Reverse bias — external «+» on the N side. The applied field reinforces the internal barrier, diffusion is blocked, and the depletion region widens — but the field is now strong enough to instantly «sweep» any stray carrier that does arrive at the junction. Both modes show up in the next two callouts.
ch1_11.insideDopingNote: One paragraph about the silicon types, since everything below leans on them. Pure silicon barely conducts current — every atom is locked into bonds with its four neighbors, leaving almost no free charges to move. To make a semiconductor useful, manufacturers add a tiny amount of impurity (about one impurity atom per ten million silicon atoms). N-type silicon is doped with atoms like phosphorus that bring one extra electron beyond what the bonds need. Those extra electrons roam freely and become mobile charge carriers — N-type silicon has electrons as its majority carriers («N» as in negative). P-type silicon is doped with atoms like boron that bring one fewer electron than the bonds need. The missing bonding spot behaves like a mobile positive particle — a «hole». P-type silicon has holes as its majority carriers («P» as in positive). Both materials are electrically neutral overall (the impurity atoms balance the carriers) — they just carry different mobile particles when you apply a voltage. In our NPN transistor: the N-type emitter and collector are packed with mobile electrons; the thin P-type base is packed with holes.

biasingDiagram.caption: An NPN transistor in active mode. The node voltages <var>V_{E}</var>, <var>V_{B}</var>, <var>V_{C}</var> are set by the external circuit; together with the doping types (N or P) they determine the bias state of each junction.
biasingDiagram.ariaLabel: Cross-section of an NPN transistor showing the three terminal voltages and the resulting bias state of each junction: base-emitter forward, base-collector reverse.

ch1_11.sectionOscillator: The third job — making it oscillate
ch1_11.oscIntro: You have made the transistor switch (fully on or off) and amplify (a small signal controls a bigger copy). Its third classic job — as fundamental as the other two — is to oscillate: to manufacture a clean, repeating signal all by itself, with no input signal at all, drawing only on the steady supply rail. Every transmitter needs one to make the carrier it sends, and every receiver needs one as the «local oscillator» that tunes it across the band (you will meet both in Part 3). So where can a signal possibly come from when nothing is feeding the input?
ch1_11.oscAnalogy: The screech you already know. Hold a microphone too close to the loudspeaker it feeds, and the PA system howls. The path is a loop: a faint sound enters the microphone, the amplifier makes it louder, the loudspeaker plays it, that louder sound re-enters the microphone, is amplified again, and within a fraction of a second a tiny rustle has snowballed into a sustained tone. Nobody is singing — the system is generating the sound itself. That runaway loop is an oscillator, and it shows the one new ingredient we need: feedback — routing a copy of the output back to the input.
ch1_11.oscMechanism: An oscillator is an amplifier with feedback. Take the common-emitter amplifier you just built and add a deliberate path from its output back to its input. Everything now hinges on the sign of that path. If the returning signal arrives out of phase — its rises and falls working against what is already at the input — it subtracts and calms the amplifier down; that is negative feedback, the same steadying role the emitter resistor played earlier in this chapter. If instead the returning signal arrives in phase — its rises and falls lined up in time with the input, reinforcing it — it adds, and any small disturbance feeds on itself and grows. That is positive feedback, and it is what makes the PA howl and what makes a transistor oscillate. The block diagram traces the whole loop:
ch1_11.oscConditions: Two conditions decide whether the loop sings. For the circuit to settle into a steady oscillation — rather than fade to silence or clip into a mess — two things must hold at once. (1) In phase. By the time a signal has travelled all the way around the loop and back to the input, it must arrive in step with the signal already there — a round-trip phase shift of 0° (or a whole number of full turns). (2) Enough gain. The amplifier must put back at least as much energy each cycle as the loop loses, so the loop gain (the amplifier's gain multiplied by the fraction fed back) must be at least 1 — a loop gain of 1 means the signal coming back is exactly as strong as the one that left, so it replaces itself perfectly. To start, the loop gain sits a hair above 1 and the signal grows. As the swing gets larger the amplifier can no longer keep up — a bigger swing runs closer to the supply rails, where there is less room to amplify — so its gain sags until the loop gain settles at exactly 1, and from then on the amplitude holds steady.
ch1_11.oscFrequency: What fixes the frequency? If the feedback path treated every frequency alike, the loop would have no reason to pick one note over another. So we put a frequency-selective network in the loop — almost always the LC tank from chapter 1.7. The tank returns the signal exactly in phase only at its resonant frequency f = 1 / (2π√(LC)); at every other frequency the phase comes back wrong and condition (1) fails. So out of a noisy jumble the loop locks onto that one frequency and rings there — the very selectivity you measured on the VNA in chapter 1.7. The higher the tank's Q factor — a measure of how sharply it favours its one resonant frequency — the more tightly it pins that frequency and the steadier the oscillator's output stays over time.
ch1_11.oscStartup: Where does the very first signal come from? Noise. Even with nothing at its input, every amplifier puts out a faint hiss of all frequencies the instant it powers up — the random thermal jostling of electrons (chapter 1.1). The tank sifts its resonant frequency out of that hiss, the in-phase loop amplifies it, and — exactly like the PA howl — it snowballs from noise into a full, clean sine wave in milliseconds. The output panel in the diagram above animates precisely this: jitter resolving into a steady tone. The amplifier's gain-sag at large amplitude is what halts the growth and holds the level constant.
ch1_11.oscCrystalVfo: Two flavours you will meet in a real rig. Change the frequency-selective element and you get the two oscillators in every transceiver. With an LC tank you can tune the frequency by turning a variable capacitor — that is the VFO (variable-frequency oscillator) that walks you across a band. Replace the tank with a thin slice of quartz — a crystal oscillator — and you trade tunability for rock-steadiness: a quartz crystal behaves like an LC tank with an enormous Q (tens of thousands, against a couple of hundred for a coil-and-capacitor tank), so its frequency barely drifts with temperature or knocks. That is why the «crystal» in a radio holds frequency so well, and why the same 32.768 kHz crystal ticks inside every quartz watch. The named textbook circuits — Colpitts, Hartley, Pierce — are just different ways of wiring up the same amplifier-plus-resonant-feedback idea; you do not need them at this level.
ch1_11.oscUnify: One device, three jobs. Notice that nothing inside the transistor changed. It is the same part, biased into the same active region as the amplifier — the only addition is a feedback path with the right phase and a resonant circuit to choose the frequency. Switch, amplifier, oscillator: three jobs from one three-legged part. That is why a single chapter on the transistor quietly unlocks the receiver and transmitter block diagrams in Part 3, where these very stages get their names and their wiring.

oscBlock.caption: An amplifier becomes an oscillator when a fraction of its output is fed back to its input in phase. The LC tank returns only its resonant frequency in phase, so the loop builds — out of the amplifier's own noise — into a steady sine wave at that one frequency. No input signal is required.
oscBlock.ariaLabel: Block diagram of a feedback oscillator. A summing junction feeds a triangular amplifier block; the amplifier output both leaves to the right as a sine wave and branches downward through an «LC tank» feedback box that returns left and up to the summing junction, closing the loop. The output waveform builds from noise into a steady sine.

ch1_11.quiz_q9: What turns an ordinary amplifier into an oscillator?
ch1_11.quiz_q9_a: Disconnecting its power supply so it runs on stored charge
ch1_11.quiz_q9_b: Cooling the transistor until its current gain <var>β</var> stops drifting
ch1_11.quiz_q9_c: Raising the collector resistor until the transistor saturates
ch1_11.quiz_q9_d: Feeding part of the output back to the input in phase
ch1_11.quiz_q9_explanation: An oscillator is just an amplifier with a deliberate feedback loop. If the returning signal arrives in phase (positive feedback) and the loop gain is at least 1, any tiny disturbance grows and the circuit generates a steady signal of its own — no input needed. Out-of-phase (negative) feedback would calm the amplifier instead.
ch1_11.quiz_q10: In an LC oscillator, what sets the frequency it oscillates at?
ch1_11.quiz_q10_a: The resonant frequency of the LC tank in the feedback path
ch1_11.quiz_q10_b: The transistor's current gain <var>β</var> in the active region
ch1_11.quiz_q10_c: The supply-rail voltage <var>V_{CC}</var> that powers the entire transmitter
ch1_11.quiz_q10_d: The amplitude of the start-up noise that gets it going
ch1_11.quiz_q10_explanation: The amplifier would happily oscillate at any frequency, so a frequency-selective network — the LC tank — decides which one. Only at the tank's resonant frequency <var>f</var> = 1/(2π√(<var>L</var><var>C</var>)) does the feedback come back exactly in phase, so that is the frequency the loop locks onto. A higher tank Q pins it more sharply; a quartz crystal does the same job with a far higher Q and far better stability.

ch2_1.heroAriaLabel: A dipole antenna on the left radiating concentric wavefronts to the right, with a sine wave running along the central axis and one wavelength marked lambda.
ch2_1.intro1: Everything in Part 1 happened inside a wire: current flowing around a loop, voltage pushing it, components shaping it. This chapter is about the moment some of that energy leaves the wire and travels through empty space. That escaped energy is a radio wave — and learning to launch it, shape it, and catch it again is the whole craft of radio.
ch2_1.intro2: You already have the key ingredient. In Chapter 1.3 you learned to make current flow back and forth — <ac>alternating current</ac>. Wiggle that current fast enough, in the right piece of wire, and a wave sets off across the room, then the building, then — with enough power — the planet, all at the speed of light. This chapter explains how that wave is born, how fast it travels, and how we measure its size.
ch2_1.fieldsP1: Before we can talk about a wave, we need one idea: a field. A field is simply a region of space where energy is stored and a force can be felt. You already live inside one — gravity. The Earth's gravitational field pulls on anything with mass; a bathroom scale is really a «gravity meter» that reads higher the heavier you are. Lift a stone onto a shelf and you store energy in it — energy the field hands straight back the moment the stone falls. A field, in short, is «a place where something would get pushed».
ch2_1.fieldsP2: Electricity comes with two such fields. An electric field surrounds anything with a voltage on it — its «mass» is electric charge, and you loaded energy into one every time you charged a capacitor in Chapter 1.5. A magnetic field surrounds anything carrying a current — the very field you wound into a coil in Chapter 1.6. Both are invisible; we only ever see their effects — a spinning motor, a warm resistor, a nail tugged toward a magnet. The whole radio story is what happens when these two fields start changing in time.
ch2_1.sectionBirth: How a radio wave is born
ch2_1.birthP1: Here is the trick that makes radio possible, worked out by James Maxwell in the 1860s and proven by Heinrich Hertz in 1886 — whose name now labels the unit of frequency. A magnetic field that is changing creates an electric field beside it; and an electric field that is changing creates a magnetic field. Each one, simply by changing, gives birth to the other.
ch2_1.birthP2: So drive a wire with <ac>alternating current</ac> — current that wiggles back and forth — and its magnetic field wiggles with it. That changing magnetic field spawns a changing electric field a little further out; that electric field spawns a magnetic field further still; and the pair leapfrogs off into space, no wire required. This self-sustaining disturbance of linked electric and magnetic fields is an <emw>electromagnetic wave</emw> — and at radio frequencies we call it a <rw>radio wave</rw>.
ch2_1.birthP3: The diagram below is one stretch of that wave, animated. The electric field E oscillates up and down; the magnetic field B oscillates side to side, at a perfect right angle to it; and the whole pattern marches to the right. The two fields are not separate things that merely overlap — they are two faces of a single object, the wave, and neither can exist without the other.

emWave.ariaLabel: An electromagnetic wave: the electric field oscillating vertically and the magnetic field oscillating horizontally at a right angle to it, both in phase, the whole pattern travelling to the right at the speed of light.

ch2_1.speedP1: Every electromagnetic wave — radio, light, X-rays alike — shares one habit: it travels at the <sol>speed of light</sol>, written <var>c</var>. In empty space (and very nearly in air) that is about 300 000 kilometres every second, or 3 × 10⁸ metres per second — fast enough to lap the Earth seven and a half times in the time it takes to say «one». Crucially, <var>c</var> does not depend on the frequency: a sleepy 1 kHz wave and a frantic 10 GHz wave leave the antenna at exactly the same speed.
ch2_1.speedP2: Waves do slow a little inside materials. In the polyethylene that fills most <coax>coaxial cable</coax> a signal travels at about two-thirds of <var>c</var> — a figure called the velocity factor, which you will meet again when you cut feedlines to length. But through air and empty space, <var>c</var> is our reliable constant.
ch2_1.wlP1: A wave can be measured two ways. The first is its <freq>frequency</freq> — how many full cycles pass a fixed point each second, the same quantity you met with the alternating current of Chapter 1.3. The second is its <wl>wavelength</wl> (<var>λ</var>) — the distance from one crest to the next. Picture a long train rolling past you at a steady speed: the frequency is how many carriages pass each second, and the wavelength is the length of one carriage. At a fixed speed, carriages that pass quickly must be short, and long carriages must pass slowly — so frequency and wavelength are just two ways of describing the same motion, bound together by the speed.
ch2_1.wlP2: For a radio wave that speed is c, which gives the single most useful equation in this chapter: λ = c / f — wavelength equals the speed of light divided by the frequency. Higher frequency, shorter wave; lower frequency, longer wave. Amateurs even name their bands by wavelength — «20 metres», «2 metres», «70 centimetres» — rather than by frequency.
ch2_1.wlP3: Because c is almost exactly 300 000 000 m/s, there is a shortcut worth committing to memory: λ in metres = 300 / f in MHz. So the 7 MHz band has a wavelength of 300 / 7 ≈ 43 m (its «40-metre» name is a round nickname, not the exact figure), while 145 MHz works out to 300 / 145 ≈ 2 m — the «2-metre» band. Try it both ways in the converter below.

lambdaF.title: Wavelength ↔ frequency
lambdaF.description: Type a frequency to get its wavelength, or a wavelength to get its frequency. The two are locked together by <var>λ</var> = <var>c</var> / <var>f</var>.
lambdaF.hint: Radio shortcut: <var>λ</var> in metres = 300 / <var>f</var> in MHz. So 14 MHz is roughly a 21-metre wave, and the 20-metre amateur band sits right around there. (Band edges are approximate, for Region 1: Europe, Africa, northern Asia.)

ch2_1.polP1: A wave's electric field has to point somewhere. Polarisation is simply the direction it oscillates, seen end-on as the wave comes toward you. If the field swings up and down, the wave is vertically polarised; if it swings side to side, horizontally polarised. Twist the wave so the field rotates as it travels and you get circular polarisation. (The magnetic field, always at its right angle, just comes along for the ride.)
ch2_1.polP2: The transmitting antenna sets the polarisation: a vertical whip on a car radiates vertically, a horizontal Yagi radiates horizontally, a helix radiates circularly. It matters because the receiving antenna should match. Aim a vertical antenna at a horizontally polarised signal — a mismatch called cross-polarisation — and you can lose more than 20 dB, over 99 % of the power. That is why local SSB operators on 2 metres agree to hold their antennas vertical, while weak-signal and satellite work follow their own conventions.
ch2_1.specP1: Radio waves are not a special kind of wave — they are just the low-frequency end of one enormous family, the electromagnetic spectrum. Climb the frequency ladder and the very same oscillating fields become infrared (which you feel as heat), then a paper-thin band of visible light, then ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. Every one of them is the same thing — linked electric and magnetic fields travelling at the speed of light; only the frequency changes.
ch2_1.specP2: The radio slice itself, from roughly 3 kHz to 300 GHz, is carved into named bands. At the low end sit the very-low, low, and medium-frequency bands; then come <hf>HF</hf> (high frequency, 3–30 MHz — the long-distance workhorse), <vhf>VHF</vhf>, <uhf>UHF</uhf>, and up. Amateurs get slices throughout — the bands the converter named above — and each behaves differently, which is the whole subject of the propagation chapter later. For now, the takeaway is one picture:

polar.caption: Polarisation seen end-on, as the wave travels toward you. The orange arrow is the electric field; its orientation is the polarisation.
polar.ariaLabel: Three end-on views of a wave coming toward the viewer, showing the electric field oriented vertically, horizontally, and rotating for circular polarisation.

spectrum.caption: The electromagnetic spectrum on a logarithmic scale. Radio is just one slice; the same fields at higher frequencies become light and beyond.
spectrum.ariaLabel: A logarithmic frequency axis from kilohertz up to 10 to the 21 hertz, showing the radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma-ray regions, with a bracket marking the amateur radio bands.

ch2_1.keyTakeaway1: A radio wave is a self-sustaining disturbance of linked electric and magnetic fields, launched when an alternating current wiggles in a wire — an antenna.
ch2_1.keyTakeaway2: The electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular and in phase — two faces of one wave, not two separate things.
ch2_1.keyTakeaway3: Every electromagnetic wave travels at the speed of light, c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s, no matter its frequency.
ch2_1.keyTakeaway4: Wavelength and frequency are tied by λ = c / f — or, for radio, the shortcut λ in metres = 300 / f in MHz.
ch2_1.keyTakeaway5: Polarisation is the orientation of the electric field, set by the transmitting antenna — the receiving antenna must match it, or much of the signal is lost.
ch2_1.keyTakeaway6: Radio is just the low-frequency end of one continuous electromagnetic spectrum — infrared, visible light, and X-rays are the same kind of wave at higher frequencies.
ch2_1.labGoal: Show that an alternating current in one wire induces a voltage in a nearby wire with nothing connecting them — the bare principle behind every antenna.
ch2_1.labComp1: Two pieces of wire, about 30 cm each
ch2_1.labStep1: Connect Arduino pin 9 to a 30 cm wire — the «transmitting» antenna — and leave its far end free.
ch2_1.labStep2: Load a sketch that toggles pin 9 as fast as the board can — tens of kHz from a simple loop, or up to a few MHz with advanced direct-port tricks. The faster it switches, the stronger the effect.
ch2_1.labStep3: Suspend the second 30 cm wire a few centimetres away, connected only to the oscilloscope probe — probe tip to the wire, ground clip to the Arduino GND.
ch2_1.labStep4: Watch the oscilloscope. With the receive wire close, a small wiggle should appear in step with the transmitted signal — energy crossing the gap with no electrical connection at all.
ch2_1.labStep5: Slowly move the receive wire away. The induced signal shrinks fast; bring it back and it returns.
ch2_1.labExpected: A few to a few tens of millivolts of induced signal at close range, dropping off quickly with distance. It is not a clean radio link — Arduino clock speeds sit far below the ham bands and the power is tiny — but it is unmistakable proof that a wiggling current in one wire reaches another across empty space.
ch2_1.labConnection: What you just built is a scaled-down version of what an <ant>antenna</ant> does. The changing current in the transmitting wire set up a changing field that reached across the gap and induced a current in the receive wire — energy crossing empty space with no connection between them. A real antenna does the same thing, but runs fast and large enough to launch that field as a self-sustaining wave that travels far beyond the bench.
ch2_1.labTrouble1: Nothing at all on the scope: make sure the oscilloscope ground clip goes to the Arduino GND. Without a shared ground reference the scope cannot read the signal.
ch2_1.labTrouble2: The signal does not change as you move the wire: you may be seeing mains hum or coupling through the bench, not your transmitter. Unplug the Arduino for a moment — if the «signal» stays, it is not coming from your wire.
ch2_1.labTrouble3: Very weak even up close: raise the toggling frequency and narrow the gap between the wires. Radiated coupling climbs steeply with frequency.
ch2_1.quiz_q1: What is a radio wave actually made of?
ch2_1.quiz_q1_a: A stream of fast electrons flying through the open air
ch2_1.quiz_q1_b: Vibrating air, just like sound but travelling faster
ch2_1.quiz_q1_c: Linked electric and magnetic fields renewing each other
ch2_1.quiz_q1_d: An electric current flowing along an invisible wire in space
ch2_1.quiz_q1_explanation: A radio wave is a self-sustaining disturbance of electric and magnetic fields — nothing physically travels across the gap, and no medium such as air is needed. It is not sound: sound is moving air and dies in a vacuum, while radio waves cross empty space happily.
ch2_1.quiz_q2: How are the electric and magnetic fields arranged inside an electromagnetic wave?
ch2_1.quiz_q2_a: At right angles, both peaking at the same instant
ch2_1.quiz_q2_b: Parallel to each other, pointing the very same way
ch2_1.quiz_q2_c: At right angles, but one peaks when the other is zero
ch2_1.quiz_q2_d: Randomly, changing direction from moment to moment
ch2_1.quiz_q2_explanation: The two fields sit at a perfect right angle and rise and fall together — they are two aspects of one wave, not separate things. The right-angle direction between them also points the way the wave travels.
ch2_1.quiz_q3: A 2 MHz wave and a 2 GHz wave both leave an antenna. Which one travels faster through space?
ch2_1.quiz_q3_a: The 2 GHz wave — a higher frequency means a higher speed
ch2_1.quiz_q3_b: The 2 MHz wave — lower frequencies travel more easily
ch2_1.quiz_q3_c: It depends on the transmitter's output power
ch2_1.quiz_q3_d: Both travel at the same speed — the speed of light
ch2_1.quiz_q3_explanation: Every electromagnetic wave travels at <var>c</var> ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s regardless of frequency. Frequency sets the wavelength, not the speed.
ch2_1.quiz_q4: Using <var>λ</var> = <var>c</var> / <var>f</var> (shortcut: 300 / <var>f</var> in MHz), what is the wavelength of a 150 MHz signal?
ch2_1.quiz_q4_explanation: 300 / 150 = 2 metres — which is why 150 MHz sits in the «2-metre» region. Higher frequency, shorter wave.
ch2_1.quiz_q5: A wave has a wavelength of 3 metres. What is its frequency?
ch2_1.quiz_q5_explanation: Rearrange the shortcut: <var>f</var> in MHz = 300 / <var>λ</var> in metres = 300 / 3 = 100 MHz.
ch2_1.quiz_q6: What determines the polarisation of a radio wave?
ch2_1.quiz_q6_a: The orientation of its electric field
ch2_1.quiz_q6_c: The frequency the wave was transmitted at
ch2_1.quiz_q6_d: The total distance the wave has travelled
ch2_1.quiz_q6_explanation: Polarisation is simply which way the electric field oscillates — vertical, horizontal, or rotating. A vertical antenna radiates a vertically polarised wave; a horizontal one radiates horizontal.
ch2_1.quiz_q7: Why does receiving a horizontally polarised signal with a vertical antenna give a weak result?
ch2_1.quiz_q7_a: Vertical antennas only work for nearby local signals
ch2_1.quiz_q7_c: Horizontally polarised waves travel noticeably slower
ch2_1.quiz_q7_d: It makes no difference — an antenna catches every polarisation
ch2_1.quiz_q7_explanation: When the antenna does not match the wave's polarisation, far less of the field pushes on its electrons. A 90° mismatch — cross-polarisation — can cut the received signal by more than 20 dB, over 99 % of the power.
ch2_1.quiz_q8: Where does radio sit in the electromagnetic spectrum?
ch2_1.quiz_q8_a: It is a completely separate phenomenon from light
ch2_1.quiz_q8_b: At the high-frequency end, above the gamma rays
ch2_1.quiz_q8_c: At the low-frequency end of one continuous spectrum
ch2_1.quiz_q8_d: Only radio is electromagnetic; the rest are particle streams
ch2_1.quiz_q8_explanation: Radio (about 3 kHz to 300 GHz) is the low-frequency slice of one continuous spectrum. Infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are electromagnetic waves too — same linked fields, same speed, only higher frequencies.

ch2_2.heroAriaLabel: A slow audio waveform on the left feeding into a fast carrier sine, whose peaks swell and shrink to trace the audio — an amplitude-modulated radio wave leaving an antenna on the right.
ch2_2.intro1: In Chapter 2.1 you learned what a radio wave is and that it flies at the speed of light. But a bare wave — a pure, unchanging sine — barely says anything. Switch it on and the only message the world receives is «I am here». This chapter is about the next step: loading real information onto that wave, so it can carry your voice, your Morse, or a stream of data across the planet.
ch2_2.intro2: The craft of doing that is called <mod>modulation</mod>. We will follow one signal all the way through: a voice, turned into electricity by a microphone, gently altering a high-frequency <car>carrier</car> so it can fly. Along the way we will meet the three classic ways radio carries a voice — <am>AM</am>, <ssb>SSB</ssb>, and <fm>FM</fm> — and see why each one occupies the slice of spectrum it does.
ch2_2.sectionMessage: The message: audio and digital signals
ch2_2.messageP1: Start with the thing you actually want to send. Sound is moving air — pressure rising and falling against your eardrum. A microphone is a tiny generator that turns those pressure waves into a voltage that rises and falls in exact step. Plot that voltage against time and you get the wiggly trace you see in any voice-memo app: an audio signal. Human speech lives almost entirely between about 300 Hz and 3 kHz — slow and low compared with the radio frequencies to come.
ch2_2.messageP2: Messages come in two flavours. Some vary smoothly through every in-between value — a voice, music. We call these analog. Others have only a few fixed states — on or off, 1 or 0. We call these digital. Morse code is the original digital signal: the key is either down or up, with nothing in between. Whichever kind it is, this raw, low-frequency information — before it touches a radio — is the baseband signal.
ch2_2.messageP3: On an oscilloscope the two look quite different — one a smooth wiggle, the other a staircase of flat steps:

audioDigital.caption: An analog signal (top) varies smoothly through every value; a digital signal (bottom) jumps between a few fixed levels. Both are «baseband» — the raw message, before modulation.
audioDigital.ariaLabel: Two stacked plots over a shared time axis: the top is a smooth wiggly analog waveform, the bottom is a square digital waveform switching between a low and a high level.

ch2_2.sectionWhy: Why a voice can't fly on its own
ch2_2.whyP1: Here is the obvious question: if the microphone already hands us an electrical signal, why not push it straight into an antenna and be done? Two reasons, and both are fatal.
ch2_2.whyP2: First, antenna size. In Chapter 2.1 we saw that an antenna must be a sizeable fraction of a wavelength to radiate well, and that wavelength is λ = c / f. Put a 3 kHz audio tone through that: λ = 300 000 000 / 3000 = 100 000 m — a wavelength of 100 km. A useful antenna would be a quarter of that, twenty-five kilometres of vertical wire. Nobody is building that.
ch2_2.whyP3: Second, everyone at once. Every human voice occupies the same band, roughly 300 Hz to 3 kHz. Wire them all straight to antennas and every station on Earth would pile into that one narrow sliver of spectrum — a single unintelligible roar, with room for just one conversation on the whole planet.

antennaSize.caption: An antenna must be a fraction of a wavelength. At an audio frequency the wavelength is tens of kilometres; shift the signal up to a radio carrier and the antenna shrinks to something you can hold.
antennaSize.ariaLabel: A size comparison: a 3 kilohertz audio signal needs a 25 kilometre antenna shown next to a tiny human figure, while a 145 megahertz radio carrier needs only a half-metre whip.

ch2_2.whyP4: The fix solves both problems at once.
